claim: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a diverse group of non-coding RNAs that direct chemical modifications at specific residues on other RNA molecules, primarily on ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
source: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a diverse group of non-coding RNAs that direct chemical modifications at specific residues on other RNA molecules, primarily on ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about snoRNAs and their function.

claim: SnoRNAs are altered in several cancers.
source: SnoRNAs are altered in several cancers; however, their role in cell homeostasis as well as in cellular transformation remains poorly explored.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature in the introduction section.

claim: Specific subsets of snoRNAs are differentially regulated during the earliest cellular response to oncogenic RASG12V expression.
source: Here, we show that specific subsets of snoRNAs are differentially regulated during the earliest cellular response to oncogenic RASG12V expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from snoRNA qPCR array analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SNORA24 guides two pseudouridine modifications within the small ribosomal subunit.
source: We describe a novel function for one H/ACA snoRNA, SNORA24, which guides two pseudouridine modifications within the small ribosomal subunit, in RAS-induced senescence in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using SCARLET to detect pseudouridine modifications at specific sites.

claim: Loss of Snora24 cooperates with RASG12V to promote the development of liver cancer in mouse models.
source: We find that in mouse models, loss of Snora24 cooperates with RASG12V to promote the development of liver cancer that closely resembles human steatohepatitic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo mouse model data showing tumor development in LNA-24 treated mice.

claim: Human HCCs with low SNORA24 expression display increased lipid content.
source: From a clinical perspective, we further show that human HCCs with low SNORA24 expression display increased lipid content and are associated with poor patient survival.
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data from human HCC specimens shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Human HCCs with low SNORA24 expression are associated with poor patient survival.
source: From a clinical perspective, we further show that human HCCs with low SNORA24 expression display increased lipid content and are associated with poor patient survival.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications exhibit perturbations in aminoacyl-transfer RNA (aa-tRNA) selection.
source: Single-molecule Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) analyses revealed that these ribosomes exhibit perturbations in aminoacyl-transfer RNA (aa-tRNA) selection and altered pre-translocation ribosome complex dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by smFRET experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications exhibit altered pre-translocation ribosome complex dynamics.
source: Single-molecule Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) analyses revealed that these ribosomes exhibit perturbations in aminoacyl-transfer RNA (aa-tRNA) selection and altered pre-translocation ribosome complex dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by smFRET experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: HCC cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications have increased translational miscoding frequencies.
source: Furthermore, we find that HCC cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications have increased translational miscoding and stop codon readthrough frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HCC cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications have increased stop codon readthrough frequencies.
source: Furthermore, we find that HCC cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications have increased translational miscoding and stop codon readthrough frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 28 H/ACA snoRNAs were dynamically changed in expression following RASG12V expression in primary fibroblasts compared to control cells (FDR < 0.1).
source: While the levels of the vast majority of H/ACA snoRNAs appeared unchanged following RASG12V expression in primary fibroblasts, we observed a dynamic change in the expression of 28 H/ACA snoRNAs compared to control cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1) (for example SNORA23, SNORA24, SNORA26, SNORA48, and SNORA67).
evidence: This is supported by snoRNA qPCR array data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The majority of H/ACA snoRNAs changed by RASG12V expression were predominately upregulated (FDR < 0.1).
source: The majority of these H/ACA snoRNAs were predominately upregulated (FDR < 0.1), with the exception of 3 snoRNAs that were downregulated (SNORA36C, SNORA53, and SNORA70B) downstream of oncogenic RAS.
evidence: This is supported by snoRNA qPCR array data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 3 snoRNAs (SNORA36C, SNORA53, and SNORA70B) were downregulated downstream of oncogenic RAS.
source: The majority of these H/ACA snoRNAs were predominately upregulated (FDR < 0.1), with the exception of 3 snoRNAs that were downregulated (SNORA36C, SNORA53, and SNORA70B) downstream of oncogenic RAS.
evidence: This is supported by snoRNA qPCR array data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in H/ACA snoRNA levels upon RASG12V expression is not associated with elevated global protein production.
source: The increase in H/ACA snoRNA levels upon RASG12V expression is not associated with elevated global protein production.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A pronounced decrease in overall protein synthesis occurs as a consequence of RAS-induced senescence.
source: On the contrary, we observe a pronounced decrease in overall protein synthesis as a consequence of RAS-induced senescence detected by monitoring O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) incorporation into newly synthesized proteins (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The change in global protein synthesis is consistent with the cell cycle arrest that occurs upon induction of senescence.
source: This change in global protein synthesis is consistent with the cell cycle arrest that occurs upon induction of senescence.
evidence: This is an inference based on known biology of senescence and the observed data.

claim: Downregulation of the tumor suppressor PTEN promotes OIS in primary cells.
source: Interestingly, downregulation of the tumor suppressor PTEN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, bottom panel), a known oncogenic event that also promotes OIS in primary cells, had no obvious effect on the expression of selective RAS-induced H/ACA snoRNAs in primary fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and highlighted in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and experimental data.

claim: Downregulation of PTEN had no obvious effect on the expression of selective RAS-induced H/ACA snoRNAs in primary fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, downregulation of the tumor suppressor PTEN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, bottom panel), a known oncogenic event that also promotes OIS in primary cells, had no obvious effect on the expression of selective RAS-induced H/ACA snoRNAs in primary fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and highlighted in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Distinct oncogenic lesions alter a unique snoRNA expression pattern during OIS.
source: These findings suggest that distinct oncogenic lesions alter a unique snoRNA expression pattern during OIS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of RASG12V and PTEN downregulation on snoRNA expression.

claim: SNORA24 is significantly decreased in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (p<1.35×10−9).
source: In the case of liver cancer, we observed an upregulation of 4 snoRNAs (SNORA14B, SNORA17, SNORA72, and SNORA81) and decreased expression of 2 H/ACA snoRNAs (SNORA24 and SNORA67) (p<10−5) in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (Figure 1C, left panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray gene expression data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SNORA67 is significantly decreased in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (p<4.6×10−7).
source: In the case of liver cancer, we observed an upregulation of 4 snoRNAs (SNORA14B, SNORA17, SNORA72, and SNORA81) and decreased expression of 2 H/ACA snoRNAs (SNORA24 and SNORA67) (p<10−5) in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (Figure 1C, left panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray gene expression data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 4 snoRNAs (SNORA14B, SNORA17, SNORA72, and SNORA81) are upregulated in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (p<10−5).
source: In the case of liver cancer, we observed an upregulation of 4 snoRNAs (SNORA14B, SNORA17, SNORA72, and SNORA81) and decreased expression of 2 H/ACA snoRNAs (SNORA24 and SNORA67) (p<10−5) in 91 primary HCC specimens compared to matched adjacent non-tumor hepatic tissue (Figure 1C, left panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray gene expression data analysis.

claim: Low levels of SNORA24 are associated with worse overall survival compared to patients with high SNORA24 expression (p=0.03, log-rank test).
source: After separating HCC patients into high or low snoRNA expression using mean ±1 standard deviation (SD) of snoRNA levels as a cutoff point, Kaplan-Meier curve analysis indicated that low levels of SNORA24 were associated with worse overall survival compared to patients with high SNORA24 expression (p=0.03, log-rank test) (Figure 1C, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Other snoRNAs assessed (including SNORA17, SNORA67, and SNORA72) did not demonstrate evidence for an association between expression levels and patient survival.
source: Interestingly, other snoRNAs assessed (including SNORA17, SNORA67, and SNORA72) did not demonstrate evidence for an association between expression levels and patient survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: SNORA24 was dramatically decreased in all HCC tumor specimens compared to non-tumor adjacent tissue by qPCR (p<0.0001) in an independent patient cohort of 13 HCC patients.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that SNORA24 was decreased in an independent patient cohort consisting of primary matched tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissue from 13 HCC patients (Supplementary file 1, samples 1–13) using qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A). Similar to our observations from microarray gene expression analysis, SNORA24 was dramatically decreased in all HCC tumor specimens compared to non-tumor adjacent tissue by qPCR (p<0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: No change in the expression of the SNORA24 host gene, SNHG8, was detected in matched tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissue.
source: In the same matched tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissue, we detected no change in the expression of the SNORA24 host gene, SNHG8 (Small Nucleolar RNA Host Gene 8) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: SNORA24 may exert a tumor suppressor role in HCC.
source: Together, these findings suggest that SNORA24 may exert a tumor suppressor role in HCC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decreased expression of SNORA24 in HCC and its association with poor survival.

claim: Hydrodynamic tail vein injection allows stable delivery of oncogenic RAS to hepatocytes using the sleeping beauty (SB) transposase system.
source: To this end, we employed a previously described mouse model of oncogenic RAS-induced senescence (Carlson et al., 2005; Kang et al., 2011) whereby hydrodynamic tail vein injection allows stable delivery of oncogenic RAS to hepatocytes using the sleeping beauty (SB) transposase system (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature describing the method.

claim: Mosaic expression of RASG12V in the mouse liver activates an anti-tumor program (OIS) to halt tumor development.
source: This model permits mosaic expression of RASG12V in the mouse liver (SB(+)NRASG12V mice) which activates an anti-tumor program (OIS) to halt tumor development (Kang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and experimental data.

claim: RASG12V promoted senescence in vivo after 6 days in SB(+)NRASG12V mice livers as measured by SA-β-galactosidase and p21 expression.
source: We confirmed that RASG12V promoted senescence in vivo after 6 days in SB(+)NRASG12V mice livers by measuring two well-characterized markers of senescence, senescence-associated (SA) β-galactosidase (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2005) and a cell cycle inhibitor p21 (Brown et al., 1997), both of which are activated downstream of mitogenic signals to halt pre-malignant cells (Collado et al., 2005; Kuilman et al., 2010) (Figure 1D, top row).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LNA-24 treatment resulted in a specific reduction in Snora24 levels in the mouse liver compared to LNA-ctrl.
source: In so doing, we observed a specific reduction in Snora24 levels in the mouse liver employing LNA-24 compared to a non-targeting scrambled sequence LNA (LNA-ctrl) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), with no observed impact on the levels of the corresponding snoRNA host gene, Snhg8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: LNA-24 treatment had no observed impact on the levels of the corresponding snoRNA host gene, Snhg8.
source: In so doing, we observed a specific reduction in Snora24 levels in the mouse liver employing LNA-24 compared to a non-targeting scrambled sequence LNA (LNA-ctrl) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), with no observed impact on the levels of the corresponding snoRNA host gene, Snhg8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Treatment with LNA-ctrl or LNA-24 had no obvious effects on hepatic tissue architecture or function.
source: Treatment with LNA-ctrl or LNA-24 had no obvious effects on hepatic tissue architecture or function (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated but data is not shown.

claim: A bypass of OIS was observed upon Snora24 reduction in SB(+)NRASG12V mice, as evident by reduced p21 expression and a lack of β-galactosidase staining (p<0.005, n = 3 mice per condition).
source: Strikingly, we observed a bypass of OIS upon Snora24 reduction in this model, as evident by reduced p21 expression and a lack of β-galactosidase staining in liver tissue from LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice compared to LNA-ctrl treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice (Figure 1D, right panel, p<0.005, n = 3 mice per condition).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LNA-24 decreased pseudouridine modifications on 18S rRNA at positions U609 and U863.
source: Importantly, LNA-24 decreased pseudouridine modifications on 18S rRNA at positions U609 and U863 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D), without impacting modifications at other sites on 18S rRNA (U105) or 28S rRNA (U1731) that not guided by SNORA24 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.

claim: LNA-24 did not impact modifications at other sites on 18S rRNA (U105) or 28S rRNA (U1731) that are not guided by SNORA24.
source: Importantly, LNA-24 decreased pseudouridine modifications on 18S rRNA at positions U609 and U863 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D), without impacting modifications at other sites on 18S rRNA (U105) or 28S rRNA (U1731) that not guided by SNORA24 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: LNA-ctrl treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice have normal livers and do not show any signs of HCC.
source: In contrast to LNA-ctrl treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice, which have normal livers and do not show any signs of HCC (Figure 2A, bottom left panel, representative image from n = 8 mice), we found that a reduction in Snora24 cooperates with RASG12V to promote the development of liver cancer in all LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice examined (Figure 2A, bottom right panel, representative image from n = 8 mice).
evidence: This is supported by liver images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A reduction in Snora24 cooperates with RASG12V to promote the development of liver cancer in all LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice examined (n = 8 mice).
source: In contrast to LNA-ctrl treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice, which have normal livers and do not show any signs of HCC (Figure 2A, bottom left panel, representative image from n = 8 mice), we found that a reduction in Snora24 cooperates with RASG12V to promote the development of liver cancer in all LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice examined (Figure 2A, bottom right panel, representative image from n = 8 mice).
evidence: This is supported by liver images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pathological analysis of liver specimens revealed the presence of HCC in LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice, with evidence of dramatic lipid accumulation and swollen hepatocytes suggestive of hepatocyte balloons, resembling human steatohepatitic HCC (SH-HCC).
source: Pathological analysis of liver specimens revealed the presence of HCC in LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice, with evidence of dramatic lipid accumulation and swollen hepatocytes suggestive of hepatocyte balloons, the pathology of which resembles human steatohepatitic HCC (SH-HCC) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SH-HCC is a subtype of liver cancer characterized by increased fat accumulation, the etiology and genetic makeup of which is poorly understood.
source: Interestingly, SH-HCC is a subtype of liver cancer characterized by increased fat accumulation, the etiology and genetic makeup of which is poorly understood (Salomao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The presence of lipids in liver tumors derived from LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice was confirmed by Oil Red O (ORO) staining (n = 3 mice, p=0.0107).
source: The presence of lipids in liver tumors derived from LNA-24 treated SB(+)NRASG12V mice was confirmed by Oil Red O (ORO) staining (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, n = 3 mice, p=0.0107).
evidence: This is supported by ORO staining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of Snora24 cooperates with oncogenic RAS to promote the development of HCC in vivo.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that loss of Snora24 cooperates with oncogenic RAS to promote the development of HCC in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the mouse model data.

claim: Cancer-associated changes in SNORA24, identified in HCC patient expression data, may play a direct role in HCC pathogenesis.
source: These data also indicate that cancer-associated changes in SNORA24, identified in HCC patient expression data (Figure 1C), may play a direct role in HCC pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mouse model data and human patient data.

claim: In established liver tumors derived from Alb-cre;KrasG12D mice, Snora24 was significantly decreased in tumor tissue compared to liver tissue from wild-type mice (n = 3 mice per condition).
source: In line with human HCC patient expression data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), we found that in established liver tumors derived from Alb-cre;KrasG12D mice, Snora24 was significantly decreased in tumor tissue compared to liver tissue from wild-type mice (Figure 2D, n = 3 mice per condition).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: sgRNA-24 KrasG12D HCC cells exhibit reduced Snora24 expression with no obvious impact on the levels of the corresponding host gene.
source: sgRNA-24 KrasG12D HCC cells exhibit reduced Snora24 expression (Figure 2E, right panel) with no obvious impact on the levels of the corresponding host gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Snora24 reduction decreased the overall survival of mice compared to controls (p=0.017) following orthotopic injection of KrasG12D HCC cells (n = 4 mice per arm).
source: Following orthotopic injection of control (Ctrl) KrasG12D HCC cells or sgRNA-24 KrasG12D HCC cells into the subcapsular region of the median liver lobe of wild-type mice, we monitored survival over a period of 4 weeks and found that Snora24 reduction, decreased the overall survival of mice compared to controls (p=0.017) (Figure 2E, left panel n = 4 mice per arm).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Snora24 has a previously uncharacterized role in the maintenance of RAS-driven HCC in vivo.
source: These findings reveal a previously uncharacterized role for Snora24 in the maintenance of RAS-driven HCC in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the orthotopic injection survival data.

claim: Tumors with low SNORA24 levels had higher lipid content compared to tumors with high SNORA24 levels using ORO staining (p=0.0453, n = 17).
source: Strikingly, we found that tumors with low SNORA24 levels had higher lipid content compared to tumors with high SNORA24 levels using ORO staining (Figure 2F, p=0.0453, n = 17).
evidence: This is supported by ORO staining data from human HCC specimens shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is a significant correlation between SNORA24 levels and lipid content in HCC.
source: These findings confirm a significant correlation between SNORA24 levels and lipid content in HCC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ORO staining data from human HCC specimens.

claim: SNORA24 reduction by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in HuH-7 cells enhanced lipid droplet formation compared to isogenic control cells.
source: We also found that SNORA24 reduction by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in an established, well-differentiated human HCC cell line, HuH-7, (HuH-7 sgRNA-24) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), also enhanced lipid droplet formation compared to isogenic control (ctrl) HuH-7 cells (HuH-7 sgRNA-ctrl) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by LipidTOX staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There is a previously unidentified connection between SNORA24 and a particular feature of lipid accumulation associated with human SH-HCC.
source: Altogether, these findings highlight a previously unidentified connection between SNORA24 and a particular feature of lipid accumulation associated with human SH-HCC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid accumulation data from mouse models and human HCC specimens.

claim: SNORA24 guides two pseudouridine modifications on the 18S rRNA component of the small (40S) ribosomal subunit, one at position U609 within helix 18 (h18) and one at U863 at the base of expansion segment 6 (ES6).
source: SNORA24 guides two pseudouridine modifications on the 18S rRNA component of the small (40S) ribosomal subunit (Boccaletto et al., 2018), one at position uridine (U) 609 (U609) within helix 18 (h18) and one at U863 at the base of expansion segment 6 (ES6) (Figure 3A, highlighted in red).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ES6 modification is distal to known functional centers of the ribosome.
source: While the ES6 modification is distal to known functional centers of the ribosome, the h18 modification is located within the functionally important, so-called '530 loop' region of the shoulder domain (Figure 3A, highlighted in pale green).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the ribosome shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The h18 modification is located within the functionally important '530 loop' region of the shoulder domain.
source: While the ES6 modification is distal to known functional centers of the ribosome, the h18 modification is located within the functionally important, so-called '530 loop' region of the shoulder domain (Figure 3A, highlighted in pale green).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the ribosome shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The shoulder domain closes towards the body of the small ribosomal subunit during the process of aminoacyl-tRNA (aa-tRNA) selection.
source: The shoulder domain closes towards the body of the small ribosomal subunit during the process of aminoacyl-tRNA (aa-tRNA) selection, bringing residue G530 (G626 in human rRNA) into direct contact with the messenger RNA (mRNA) codon-tRNA anticodon pair such that it directly contributes to mRNA decoding (Demeshkina et al., 2012; Fislage et al., 2018; Loveland et al., 2016; Ogle et al., 2001; Ogle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on ribosome structure and function.

claim: Residue G530 (G626 in human rRNA) is brought into direct contact with the mRNA codon-tRNA anticodon pair during aa-tRNA selection such that it directly contributes to mRNA decoding.
source: The shoulder domain closes towards the body of the small ribosomal subunit during the process of aminoacyl-tRNA (aa-tRNA) selection, bringing residue G530 (G626 in human rRNA) into direct contact with the messenger RNA (mRNA) codon-tRNA anticodon pair such that it directly contributes to mRNA decoding (Demeshkina et al., 2012; Fislage et al., 2018; Loveland et al., 2016; Ogle et al., 2001; Ogle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on ribosome structure and function.

claim: SCARLET revealed diminished pseudouridine levels at both residue 609 and 863 on 18S rRNA in HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells compared to isogenic HuH-7 sgRNA-ctrl cells (>90% reduction).
source: As expected, SCARLET revealed the amount of uridine (U) and pseudouridine (Ψ) present at both residue 609 and 863 on 18S rRNA and confirmed diminished pseudouridine levels at both sites in HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells compared to isogenic HuH-7 sgRNA-ctrl cells (>90% reduction) (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SCARLET data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant change in global protein production was detected in cells lacking SNORA24-guided modifications as measured by OPP incorporation into newly synthesized protein.
source: Interestingly, we did not detect any significant change in global protein production in cells lacking SNORA24-guided modifications as measured by OPP incorporation into newly synthesized protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No detectable difference in the abundance of ribosome subunits or the abundance and distribution of polysome was observed in HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells compared to isogenic HuH-7 sgRNA-ctrl cells by sucrose gradient fractionation trace.
source: Furthermore, we saw no detectable difference in the abundance of ribosome subunits or the abundance and distribution of polysome in HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells compared to isogenic HuH-7 sgRNA-ctrl cells by sucrose gradient fractionation trace (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SNORA24 and SNORA24-guided rRNA modifications are likely dispensable for ribosome biogenesis and global protein production in HCC.
source: These results indicate that SNORA24 and SNORA24-guided rRNA modifications are likely dispensable for ribosome biogenesis and global protein production in HCC and instead may harbor specific functions during translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of changes in global protein synthesis and polysome profiles.

claim: SNORA24 and SNORA24-guided rRNA modifications may harbor specific functions during translation.
source: These results indicate that SNORA24 and SNORA24-guided rRNA modifications are likely dispensable for ribosome biogenesis and global protein production in HCC and instead may harbor specific functions during translation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: Ribosomes purified from HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells were ~50% more efficient in aa-tRNA selection of tRNAPhe compared to ribosomes isolated from sgRNA-ctrl cells (p<10−6, Welch's t-test) (kcat/KM of 50 ± 7 µM−1 s−1 vs. 71 ± 4 µM−1 s−1, respectively).
source: In doing so, we found that ribosomes purified from HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells were ~50% more efficient in aa-tRNA selection of tRNAPhe compared to ribosomes isolated from sgRNA-ctrl cells (p<10−6, Welch's t-test) (kcat/KM of 50 ± 7 µM−1 s−1 vs. 71 ± 4 µM−1 s−1, respectively) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by smFRET data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Ribosomes lacking Ψ609 and Ψ863 were ~30% more efficient in selection of tRNALys compared to their wild-type counterparts (p<10−6, Welch's t-test) (kcat/KM of 27 ± 5 µM−1 s−1 vs. 36 ± 5 µM−1 s−1).
source: Specifically, ribosomes from HuH-7 sgRNA-24 cells were ~30% more efficient in selection of tRNALys compared to their wild-type counterparts (p<10−6, Welch's t-test) (kcat/KM of 27 ± 5 µM−1 s−1 vs. 36 ± 5 µM−1 s−1) (Figure 4D) as opposed to the ~50% differences observed in the case of tRNAPhe.
evidence: This is supported by smFRET data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SNORA24-directed rRNA pseudouridylation acts to regulate decoding on actively translating ribosomes.
source: These findings indicate that SNORA24-directed rRNA pseudouridylation acts to regulate decoding on actively translating ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smFRET data showing differences in aa-tRNA selection efficiency.

claim: Ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided modifications exhibit a modest preference for classical tRNA configurations compared to control ribosomes (15 ± 1% vs. 20 ± 1% Classical, p<10−6, Welch's t-test).
source: These analyses revealed that ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided modifications exhibit a modest preference for classical tRNA configurations compared to control ribosomes (15 ± 1% vs. 20 ± 1% Classical, p<10−6, Welch's t-test) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by smFRET data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Little to no change in tRNA configurations was observed between ribosomes from sgRNA-ctrl and sgRNA-24 cells bearing Met-Lys-tRNALys in the A site.
source: In the case of ribosomes bearing Met-Lys-tRNALys in the A site, we instead observed little to no change in tRNA configurations between the two types of ribosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pseudouridine modifications at rRNA residues 609 and 863 have the capacity to alter the dynamic properties of pre-translocation ribosome complexes in a way that likely depends on the tRNA species in the P and A sites.
source: These findings indicate that pseudouridine modifications at rRNA residues 609 and 863 have the capacity to alter the dynamic properties of pre-translocation ribosome complexes in a way that likely depends on the tRNA species in the P and A sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smFRET data showing tRNA-dependent differences in ribosome dynamics.

claim: Ribosomes lacking these two specific pseudouridine modifications exhibit functionally relevant physical distinctions in regard to dynamic structural features within the pre-translocation complex, that appear to depend on the mRNA coding sequence.
source: Taken together, these smFRET data provide compelling evidence that ribosomes lacking these two specific pseudouridine modifications exhibit functionally relevant physical distinctions in regard to dynamic structural features within the pre-translocation complex, that appear to depend on the mRNA coding sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smFRET data.

claim: HCC cells lacking SNORA24 displayed a specific and increased tolerance to Anisomycin (ANS), a drug that binds to the ribosomal A site and inhibits peptidyl transfer.
source: In doing so, we found that HCC cells lacking SNORA24 displayed a specific and increased tolerance to Anisomycin (ANS), a drug that binds to the ribosomal A site (Hansen et al., 2003) and inhibits peptidyl transfer (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The increased tolerance to Anisomycin in cells lacking SNORA24 is in agreement with the smFRET observations that loss of SNORA24-guided modifications increase the efficiency of aa-tRNA selection.
source: This result is in perfect agreement with our smFRET observations that loss of SNORA24-guided modifications increase the efficiency of aa-tRNA selection, which would be expected to reduce the time window during each elongation cycle that the ribosome is sensitive to ANS.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the drug sensitivity data to the smFRET data.

claim: SnoRNA-mediated changes in the chemical composition of mammalian ribosomes have the potential to affect tRNA selection, ribosome dynamics, and sensitivity of cancer cells to specific translation inhibitors.
source: Collectively, these investigations provide compelling evidence that snoRNA-mediated changes in the chemical composition of mammalian ribosomes, have the potential to affect tRNA selection, ribosome dynamics, and sensitivity of cancer cells to specific translation inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the smFRET and drug sensitivity data.

claim: Reduced SNORA24 expression had no observed impact on overall protein production.
source: Given that reduced SNORA24 expression had no observed impact on overall protein production (Figure 3C and D), we predicted that the differences in aa-tRNA selection and conformational dynamics observed by smFRET in ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications may impact the accuracy of translation, in a codon-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation and polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The differences in aa-tRNA selection and conformational dynamics observed by smFRET in ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications may impact the accuracy of translation, in a codon-specific manner.
source: Given that reduced SNORA24 expression had no observed impact on overall protein production (Figure 3C and D), we predicted that the differences in aa-tRNA selection and conformational dynamics observed by smFRET in ribosomes lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications may impact the accuracy of translation, in a codon-specific manner.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation based on the smFRET data.

claim: HCC cells with reduced SNORA24 expression display a 10–20% increased level of amino acid misincorporation compared to control cells for both codons tested (CGC and AAU).
source: For both codons tested, we found that HCC cells with reduced SNORA24 expression display a 10–20% increased level of amino acid misincorporation compared to control cells (Figure 5A, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the presence of paromomycin, a ~15% increase in UGA stop codon readthrough was observed in cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of paromomycin, an antibiotic known to induce translation error and stop codon readthrough (Kramer et al., 2010), we observe a SNORA24-dependent increase (~15%) in UGA stop codon readthrough (Figure 5B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No difference in UAG stop codon readthrough was detected in cells lacking SNORA24-guided pseudouridine modifications.
source: By contrast, we detected no difference in UAG stop codon readthrough in the same cells (Figure 5B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ψ609 and Ψ863 within the small ribosomal subunit function to enhance translational accuracy.
source: These findings suggest that Ψ609 and Ψ863 within the small ribosomal subunit function to enhance translational accuracy and that reduced expression and activity of SNORA24 in HCC may lead to errors in the translation of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the luciferase reporter assay data showing increased miscoding and readthrough.

claim: Reduced expression and activity of SNORA24 in HCC may lead to errors in the translation of specific mRNAs.
source: These findings suggest that Ψ609 and Ψ863 within the small ribosomal subunit function to enhance translational accuracy and that reduced expression and activity of SNORA24 in HCC may lead to errors in the translation of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: Ribosome dysfunction and alterations in translation are linked to cancer development.
source: Ribosome dysfunction and alterations in translation are linked to cancer development (Pelletier et al., 2018; Silvera et al., 2010; Sulima et al., 2017; Truitt and Ruggero, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The function of the vast majority of conserved RNA modifications within the ribosome in cancer development remain largely unexplored.
source: The function of the vast majority of conserved RNA modifications within the ribosome (Decatur and Fournier, 2002), in this context remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: In unicellular organisms, depletion of individual snoRNAs yield little to no growth defect.
source: For decades, snoRNAs have been thought to exert minor functions, largely due to findings that in unicellular organisms, depletion of individual snoRNAs yield little to no growth defect.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about snoRNAs in unicellular organisms.

claim: The biological influence of snoRNA-directed rRNA modifications in mammalian physiology, and in disease states has been poorly understood.
source: In this respect, the biological influence of snoRNA-directed rRNA modifications in mammalian physiology, and in disease states has been poorly understood (Williams and Farzaneh, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: One H/ACA snoRNA plays a direct role in specific steps of cancer development.
source: We provide evidence that one H/ACA snoRNA plays a direct role in specific steps of cancer development.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SNORA24 is implicated in a tumor suppressor program in vivo to halt cellular transformation.
source: Our studies reveal that SNORA24 is implicated in a tumor suppressor program in vivo to halt cellular transformation and with compelling human and mouse data supports a role for SNORA24 dysfunction in tumor initiation and in maintenance of RAS-driven cancer.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SNORA24 dysfunction plays a role in tumor initiation and in maintenance of RAS-driven cancer.
source: Our studies reveal that SNORA24 is implicated in a tumor suppressor program in vivo to halt cellular transformation and with compelling human and mouse data supports a role for SNORA24 dysfunction in tumor initiation and in maintenance of RAS-driven cancer.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In the context of HCC, SNORA24 appears dispensable for overall protein synthesis.
source: Interestingly, in the context of HCC, SNORA24 appears dispensable for overall protein synthesis, suggesting that cancer-associated changes in SNORA24 may have more selective functions, for example towards controlling translation of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of changes in global protein synthesis.

claim: Cancer-associated changes in SNORA24 may have more selective functions, for example towards controlling translation of specific mRNAs.
source: Interestingly, in the context of HCC, SNORA24 appears dispensable for overall protein synthesis, suggesting that cancer-associated changes in SNORA24 may have more selective functions, for example towards controlling translation of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: The apparent codon specificity in aa-tRNA selection and pre-translocation complex dynamics observed by smFRET analysis supports the idea that SNORA24 may have selective functions.
source: This is supported by the apparent codon specificity in aa-tRNA selection and pre-translocation complex dynamics observed by smFRET analysis of ribosomes from cancer cells lacking SNORA24-dependent pseudouridine modifications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smFRET data showing tRNA-dependent differences.

claim: SNORA24-guided modifications may directly impinge on the production of proteins involved in lipid metabolism and signaling.
source: One intriguing possibility is that SNORA24-guided modifications directly impinge on the production of proteins involved in, for example, lipid metabolism and signaling, due to the strong association between SNORA24 and tumor lipid deposition identified in this study.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed association between SNORA24 and lipid content.

claim: There is a previous link between distinct C/D snoRNAs and response to metabolic stress.
source: It is interesting to note a previous link between distinct C/D snoRNAs and response to metabolic stress (Jinn et al., 2015; Michel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The roles of C/D snoRNAs in modulating ribosome activity or translation in the context of metabolic stress was not examined in previous studies.
source: Although the roles of C/D snoRNAs in modulating ribosome activity or translation in this context was not examined, it will be important to determine whether dysfunction of specific snoRNAs and site-specific ribosome modifications are implicated in human lipid metabolic disorders and/or in the progression of chronic liver disease to HCC.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior studies and future research directions.

claim: It will be important to determine whether dysfunction of specific snoRNAs and site-specific ribosome modifications are implicated in human lipid metabolic disorders and/or in the progression of chronic liver disease to HCC.
source: Although the roles of C/D snoRNAs in modulating ribosome activity or translation in this context was not examined, it will be important to determine whether dysfunction of specific snoRNAs and site-specific ribosome modifications are implicated in human lipid metabolic disorders and/or in the progression of chronic liver disease to HCC.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: The studies employing smFRET imaging represent the first report of biophysical changes in ribosomes from cancer cells lacking specific rRNA nucleotide modifications.
source: Our studies employing smFRET imaging represent, to our knowledge, the first report of biophysical changes in ribosomes from cancer cells lacking specific rRNA nucleotide modifications.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Ψ609 is located in a highly structured element (the '530 loop' in bacteria), a region of rRNA directly implicated in codon-anticodon pair recognition in the ribosomal A site.
source: Ψ609 is located in a highly structured element (the so-called '530 loop' in bacteria), a region of rRNA directly implicated in codon-anticodon pair recognition in the ribosomal A site.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the ribosome.

claim: Previous studies implicate the '530 loop' region as contributing to the process of domain closure, a large-scale movement within the small subunit that aids mRNA codon-tRNA anticodon pairing required for accurate decoding at the A site.
source: Previous studies implicate this region as contributing to the process of domain closure, a large-scale movement within the small subunit that aids mRNA codon-tRNA anticodon pairing required for accurate decoding at the A site (Fislage et al., 2018; Loveland et al., 2016; Ogle et al., 2001; Ogle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The data demonstrating that loss of Ψ609 and Ψ863 enhances the efficiency of aa-tRNA accommodation imply that SNORA24-guided modifications may function to alter domain closure strength.
source: Our data demonstrating that loss of Ψ609 and Ψ863 enhances the efficiency of aa-tRNA accommodation, imply that SNORA24-guided modifications, and Ψ609 in particular, may function to alter domain closure strength.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smFRET data and structural knowledge.

claim: Ψ863 is located in an rRNA expansion segment (ES) that is distal to the decoding center of the ribosome.
source: In contrast to Ψ609, Ψ863 is located in an rRNA expansion segment (ES) that is distal to the decoding center of the ribosome.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the ribosome.

claim: A recent study has established a connection between ribosome expansion segments and translation fidelity.
source: Interestingly, a recent study has established a connection between ribosome expansion segments and translation fidelity (Fujii et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It seems plausible that the functional alterations observed in ribosomes lacking Ψ609 and Ψ863 may arise from both direct and indirect mechanisms that alter how the small subunit of the ribosome recognizes and responds to aa-tRNA binding at the A site.
source: Thus, it seems plausible that the functional alterations observed in ribosomes lacking Ψ609 and Ψ863 may arise from both direct and indirect mechanisms that alter how the small subunit of the ribosome recognizes and responds to aa-tRNA binding at the A site.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and structural knowledge.

claim: The efficiency of aa-tRNA selection varies depending on the tRNA species and the codon in the A site.
source: For instance, studies have shown that the efficiency of aa-tRNA selection varies depending on the tRNA species and the codon in the A site (Pavlov and Ehrenberg, 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The stability of intermediates in the decoding process are affected by even small differences in interaction energy between the ribosome and the tRNA substrate.
source: These and other observations indicate that the stability of intermediates in the decoding process are affected by even small differences in interaction energy between the ribosome and the tRNA substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior literature.

claim: Pseudouridylation of U609 and U863 may fine tune decoding in a manner that results in small, but significant codon-dependent effects on tRNA selection efficiency.
source: We therefore speculate that pseudouridylation of U609 and U863 may fine tune decoding in a manner that results in small, but significant codon-dependent effects on tRNA selection efficiency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and prior knowledge.

claim: Factors such as tRNA abundance, codon-anticodon base pair interactions, and codon context are known to influence ribosome elongation rate and translation efficiency.
source: In addition, it seems likely that factors such as tRNA abundance, codon-anticodon base pair interactions, and codon context, that are known to influence ribosome elongation rate and translation efficiency (Gardin et al., 2014; Goodarzi et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2014; Quax et al., 2015; Riba et al., 2019), may lead to gene-specific alterations in translational control in cancer cells with altered SNORA24 expression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Factors such as tRNA abundance, codon-anticodon base pair interactions, and codon context may lead to gene-specific alterations in translational control in cancer cells with altered SNORA24 expression.
source: In addition, it seems likely that factors such as tRNA abundance, codon-anticodon base pair interactions, and codon context, that are known to influence ribosome elongation rate and translation efficiency (Gardin et al., 2014; Goodarzi et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2014; Quax et al., 2015; Riba et al., 2019), may lead to gene-specific alterations in translational control in cancer cells with altered SNORA24 expression.
evidence: This is speculation based on prior knowledge and the observed data.

claim: The finding that a distinct snoRNA impacts translational accuracy is in line with observations in other organisms, demonstrating that clusters of snoRNA-directed modifications close to the decoding center influence translational fidelity.
source: Our findings that a distinct snoRNA impacts translational accuracy is in line with observations in other organisms, demonstrating that clusters of snoRNA-directed modifications close to the decoding center influence translational fidelity (Baudin-Baillieu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Single-celled organisms can tolerate relatively high levels of translation errors.
source: However, unlike single-celled organisms that can tolerate relatively high levels of translation errors, minor defects in translation accuracy arising from snoRNA dysfunction in mammals may yield more severe cellular consequences in certain contexts, for example in response to oncogenic stress.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Minor defects in translation accuracy arising from snoRNA dysfunction in mammals may yield more severe cellular consequences in certain contexts, for example in response to oncogenic stress.
source: However, unlike single-celled organisms that can tolerate relatively high levels of translation errors, minor defects in translation accuracy arising from snoRNA dysfunction in mammals may yield more severe cellular consequences in certain contexts, for example in response to oncogenic stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and knowledge of mammalian biology.

claim: Alterations in aa-tRNA selection efficiency or fidelity during translation elongation may lead to changes in the abundance of specific proteins beneficial to cancer cell survival.
source: For instance, alterations in aa-tRNA selection efficiency or fidelity during translation elongation may lead to changes in the abundance of specific proteins beneficial to cancer cell survival.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential consequences of altered translation fidelity.

claim: Differences in translation fidelity may alter stop codon readthrough during translation termination.
source: Differences in translation fidelity may also alter stop codon readthrough during translation termination, as well as the rate at which ribosomes translocate through a given mRNA open reading frame due to impacts on translocation (Alejo and Blanchard, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Differences in translation fidelity may alter the rate at which ribosomes translocate through a given mRNA open reading frame due to impacts on translocation.
source: Differences in translation fidelity may also alter stop codon readthrough during translation termination, as well as the rate at which ribosomes translocate through a given mRNA open reading frame due to impacts on translocation (Alejo and Blanchard, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Elucidating the structural-functional roles of modified residues within the ribosome will aid in the development of a new generation of cancer therapeutics focused on targeting ribosomes with differential modification patterns in cancer.
source: Elucidating the structural-functional roles of modified residues within the ribosome will undoubtedly aid in the development of a new generation of cancer therapeutics focused on targeting ribosomes with differential modification patterns in cancer and will shed significant new light on the role of ancient RNA modifications in directing ribosome activity and cellular integrity.
evidence: This is speculation about the future implications of the research.

source: Elucidating the structural-functional roles of modified residues within the ribosome will undoubtedly aid in the development of a new generation of cancer therapeutics focused on targeting ribosomes with differential modification patterns in cancer and will shed significant new light on the role of ancient RNA modifications in directing ribosome activity and cellular integrity.
